To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) there was no consistent reduction in common childhood illnesses in relation to improvements in housing infrastructure in Indigenous communities in Australia; 2) while there were strong associations between improved infrastructure and improvements in the hygienic condition, there were only small improvements in crowding; 3) the high levels of crowding and poor socioeconomic conditions in Indigenous communities appear to constrain the potential for building to improve the health of children.
there was a strong association between improvement of housing infrastructure and improvement of the hygienic condition in the house.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of housing improvement on common childhood illnesses in a cohort of children living in Indigenous communities in Australia.
the impact of housing improvement on common childhood illnesses and the mediating factors in the relationship.
the impact of the improvement in the notoriously substandard housing infrastructure in Australian indigenous communities on the incidence of common childhood illnesses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is insufficient evidence to support the hypothesis that improvement of the notoriously poor housing stock in Australian Indigenous communities will result in reduced incidence of common childhood illnesses.
there is no conclusive evidence that housing improvements reduce common childhood illnesses.
the study found that there was no evidence to suggest that the improvement in the infrastructure of the houses in these communities had any impact on the incidence of common childhood illnesses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
housing improvements in Indigenous Australian communities are associated with improvements in hygienic condition but not with reductions in common childhood illness.
the housing improvements did not reduce common childhood illness, however there were significant associations with the hygienic state and crowding.
the improvements in the notoriously poor infrastructure in Australian Indigenous homes did not result in a reduction in common childhood illnesses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of housing on the health of children living in these communities may be constrained by other environmental and social factors.
housing improvement alone is unlikely to be an effective strategy in improving the health of Indigenous Australians.

the impact of housing improvement programs on the health of Indigenous Australians is likely to be constrained by the high levels of social disadvantage and poor socio-environmental conditions that exist in many communities.
